claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has high stacking-fault energy.
The alloy's stacking-fault energy and lattice characteristics promote rapid dislocation glide.
Rapid dislocation glide enables active dynamic recovery in this alloy.
Dynamic recovery prevents the dislocation-density buildup needed for significant work hardening.
Conventional casting and annealing can produce equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi as a single-phase solid solution with relatively coarse grains and low initial dislocation density.
Cryogenic testing near -196 °C will suppress dynamic recovery relative to room-temperature quasi-static loading.
Pre-straining can enhance the dislocation density or alter the dislocation forest.
High stacking-fault energy facilitates dislocation cross-slip and efficient recovery during deformation.
At room temperature, dynamic recovery causes rapid dislocation rearrangement and annihilation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Suppressing dynamic recovery permits greater dislocation storage.
Greater dislocation storage increases work hardening, hardness, and strength.
Cryogenic testing will produce a significant increase in hardness and strength relative to the room-temperature baseline.
Cryogenically tested specimens will have a higher dislocation density observable by TEM than room-temperature-tested specimens.
The proposed mechanism applies to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state without significant precipitates or secondary phases and under quasi-static loading.
Minor microstructural heterogeneities and grain-boundary characteristics may affect the changes in hardness and strength.
Room-temperature and cryogenic test groups should begin with identical microstructures and be tested at quasi-static strain rates.

The dynamic-recovery hypothesis is falsified if suppressing recovery produces neither a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength nor an appreciable increase in dislocation density.

contradictions.description: The comparison is required to use identical starting microstructures, but the alternative pre-strain arm necessarily changes the starting dislocation structure before testing. The cryogenic and pre-strain comparisons therefore cannot both satisfy the stated identical-microstructure control.

Pre-straining is described both as enhancing or altering the dislocation forest and as inhibiting dynamic recovery, although the hypothesis does not establish that pre-straining suppresses recovery rather than merely changing the initial dislocation density. It is therefore not mechanistically equivalent to the cryogenic intervention as stated.
